name: Confusion matrix
seoDesc: Confusion matrix: work out false negative from the accuracy and the precision. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the accuracy, the precision, the recall and the true negative rate and the Confusion matrix calculator solves for false negative. It is built for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Confusion matrix calculator work?
sections.html:
The Confusion matrix calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports false negative in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the accuracy, the precision, the recall and the true negative rate.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Confusion matrix calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

False negative=(-accuracy × (false positive + true negative + true positive) + true negative + true positive) ÷ accuracy
False positive=-true positive + true positive ÷ precision
False negative=-true positive + true positive ÷ recall
F 1 score=2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall)
False negative=-true positive + true positive ÷ true positive rate
False positive=-true negative + true negative ÷ true negative rate

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take True positive = 10, False positive = 10, True negative = 10 and Accuracy = 10 .. The calculator returns False negative = 170, Precision = 50 ., Recall = 5.5556 . and F 1 score = 10 ..

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: False negative = 170, Precision = 50 ., Recall = 5.5556 . and F 1 score = 10 . should be roughly the size you expected from True positive = 10 and False positive = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Confusion matrix calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the accuracy, the precision and the recall — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Confusion matrix calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns false negative, derived from the accuracy, the precision and the recall. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Confusion matrix calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the accuracy, the precision, the recall and the true negative rate, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter accuracy in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Accuracy opens in decimals and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports False negative = 170. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Confusion matrix calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
